slides: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of division and remainders. Everything important, in a few minutes.

slides.say: Two, five and ten, look at the last digit. Three and nine, the digit sum. Four, the last two digits, and eight, the last three.
Eleven, go plus, minus, plus, minus, digit by digit. Nine thirteen, nine minus one plus three is eleven, so it divides by eleven.
A bigger divisor? Split it into parts with no common factor. Thirty-six is four times nine, not six times six.

A number is the divisor times the quotient, plus the remainder, and the remainder is always smaller than the divisor. So the biggest remainder is the divisor minus one. And five divided by eight leaves five, not three.
Dividing by three or nine, the remainder is the same as the digit sum's. Four thousand eight hundred twenty-six, the digit sum is twenty, and twenty divided by nine leaves two.

Only the remainders matter. a leaves five and b leaves seven, dividing by eight. a plus b, five plus seven is twelve, so it leaves four. a times b, five times seven is thirty-five, so it leaves three. a minus b, five minus seven is negative two, so add eight, six.
Take away the remainder, and what's left divides exactly.
A new divisor? It must divide the old one. Leaves eleven by twelve? By four, eleven leaves three. But from ten to four, you can't know.
A fraction of a fraction? Multiply the denominators. How many multiples in a range? The last minus the first, plus one, because both ends count.
Two in a row always divide by two, and three in a row by six. And a cubed minus a is three in a row in disguise.

Necessarily divisible? Tag each condition, and read the number in front. And when you plug in, give different letters different values, avoid values that give zero, and remember that one failing example knocks a choice out.
Before each question, ask yourself. Parts with no common factor? Is my remainder smaller than the divisor? A negative remainder? Add the divisor. And does the new divisor divide the old one?
That's it. Now go practice, and I'll see you in the next video.
